articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and Issues New FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 16, 2026, issued an amended Venezuela-related General License (GL) and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This action updates existing guidance concerning sanctions programs targeting Venezuela.

The specific details of the amendments and the new FAQ were not immediately released, but such updates typically clarify permissible activities or modify restrictions under the Venezuela sanctions regime. Businesses and individuals engaging in transactions related to Venezuela are advised to review the updated guidance carefully.
These changes reflect OFAC's ongoing efforts to calibrate sanctions to achieve policy objectives while minimizing unintended humanitarian or economic impacts.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related and Cuba Designations, Issues New and Amended General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations related to Iran and a designation related to Cuba on October 15, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses (GLs) and Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) to accompany these actions.

While specific details of the designated entities and individuals were not immediately provided, the action indicates a continued focus on restricting activities deemed to support the Iranian regime and the Cuban government.

The issuance of new and amended GLs and FAQs suggests that OFAC is also providing guidance to ensure that certain humanitarian or otherwise permissible transactions can continue under the updated sanctions framework.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation on October 14, 2026. This action indicates a de-listing of an individual or entity previously subject to sanctions under the Venezuela program.
Designation removals can occur for various reasons, including a change in circumstances, a determination that the criteria for designation are no longer met, or as a result of diplomatic engagement.
Such removals can signal a recalibration of sanctions policy or a response to specific actions taken by the delisted party.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial networks supporting drug trafficking and terrorist organizations globally.
These designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating transnational criminal and terrorist threats by cutting off their access to the international financial system.
The specific individuals and entities designated were not detailed in the initial announcement, but such actions typically involve asset freezes and prohibitions on transactions with U.S. persons.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces International Criminal Court Designation and General Licenses; Burma-Related Designation Removal
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a designation related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and issued associated General Licenses on October 9, 2026. This action follows previous U.S. government concerns regarding the ICC's jurisdiction and actions.
Concurrently, OFAC also announced a removal of a Burma-related designation, indicating a potential shift in sanctions policy or a response to developments within Burma.
The issuance of General Licenses alongside the ICC designation suggests an effort to narrowly tailor the impact of the sanctions while still addressing U.S. policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License (GL) on October 9, 2026. This GL provides authorization for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the Russia sanctions program.

General Licenses are frequently used by OFAC to carve out specific activities from broader sanctions, often to facilitate humanitarian aid, certain financial transactions, or the wind-down of operations.
The details of this new GL will be crucial for entities and individuals navigating the complex landscape of Russia sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues New Iran and Amended Russia General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities deemed to be supporting the Iranian regime or its illicit activities.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License (GL) and an amended Russia-related GL. The new Iran GL likely permits certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, while the amended Russia GL adjusts existing authorizations.
These simultaneous actions highlight OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions, combining restrictive measures with tailored authorizations to achieve specific policy outcomes.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Designations Removals and Updates, Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced several designation removals and updates on October 5, 2026. These actions indicate a recalibration of existing sanctions lists.

Significantly, OFAC also published an Iran-related Alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). The Alert warns foreign financial institutions that continue to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions that they could be targeted at any time without advance notification.

The amended FAQ 156 removes language suggesting OFAC would generally contact an FFI about its conduct before making a finding of sanctionable activity, emphasizing the heightened risk for foreign financial institutions with Iranian exposure.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Global Sanctions and Export Controls Blog

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new counter terrorism designations on October 2, 2026. These actions target individuals and entities involved in supporting global terrorist activities.
These designations aim to disrupt the financial networks of terrorist organizations, preventing them from accessing funds and resources necessary for their operations.
The U.S. government continues to prioritize combating terrorism through financial sanctions, working to isolate those who facilitate or engage in such activities.

articles.headline: EU Adopts Largest-Ever Sanctions Package Against Russia's Military-Industrial Complex and DPRK Programs
body: The European Union adopted its largest-ever package of sanctions listings on October 13, 2026, targeting 1,569 individuals and entities linked to Russia's military-industrial complex.

This extensive package includes 826 Russian companies and 743 CEOs, bringing the total number of listings under the EU's Russia sanctions regime to nearly 4,600. The measures aim to disrupt the supply chains sustaining Russia's war against Ukraine.

Additionally, the EU adopted separate restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities under its autonomous sanctions regime on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), addressing its weapons programs and evasion of UN sanctions, as well as growing military and economic cooperation between DPRK and Russia.
articles.source: European External Action Service (EEAS) / Hill Dickinson

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 in OFAC Settlement for Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026, resulting in a civil monetary penalty of $11,662,930.
This settlement addresses apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, global terrorism, and narcotics.
The OFAC penalty was part of a coordinated enforcement action by the Treasury Department, which also included significant fines from FinCEN and the OCC for anti-money laundering failures.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC for $175,015

This settlement resolves apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations, though the specific nature of the violations was not detailed in the initial announcement.

Companies involved in international logistics are frequently subject to OFAC scrutiny to ensure compliance with sanctions programs, particularly concerning the movement of goods to or from sanctioned jurisdictions or entities.

articles.headline: US Inflation Jumps in September, Driven by Gasoline Prices, Core Inflation Also Rises
body: US annual consumer inflation rose to 3.7% in September from 3.4% in August, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
A 9.1% jump in gasoline prices accounted for more than half of the overall rise, with energy prices 20.4% higher than a year earlier.

In a worrying sign for central bankers, core inflation, which excludes food and energy costs, also accelerated to 2.6% from 2.4%, indicating that inflationary pressures may be broadening beyond just energy.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty Against Bank of America for BSA/AML Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026, for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and its implementing regulations.

This penalty is the largest in OCC history and stems from the bank's deficient and ineffective BSA/AML compliance program, which included systemic internal-control gaps, weak independent testing, and inadequate BSA/AML training.

The OCC found that Bank of America failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, resulting in a large number of missed, late, inaccurate, and incomplete Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars in suspicious activities.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
